claims.text: The catalyst is a platinum-group-metal-based nanoscale catalyst for ethanol oxidation.
The catalyst has a relatively homogeneous native oxidation-state distribution before intervention.
High ethanol-oxidation performance arises from synergy between dynamically distributed, heterogeneous surface oxidation states.
Adjacent oxidized and reduced sites facilitate sequential adsorption and processing of ethanol-derived intermediates.
The proposed dual-site arrangement promotes dehydrogenation and C–C bond cleavage.
The proposed dual-site arrangement mitigates catalyst poisoning.
Potential cycling or minor alloying with an electron-density-shifting element can promote heterogeneous surface oxidation states relative to steady-state operation.
Moderate potentials permit accessible surface oxidation-state dynamics without causing bulk oxidation or irreversible structural changes.
Adjacent sites having different oxidation states mediate enhanced adsorption and sequential conversion of ethanol-derived intermediates.
Oxidized surface sites preferentially adsorb oxygenated intermediates.
Adjacent reduced sites facilitate dehydrogenation and C–C bond cleavage.
Cooperation between oxidized and reduced sites lowers kinetic barriers.
A multication high-entropy perovskite oxide exhibits an intrinsic composition–activity relationship and higher OER activity than its single-B-site parent compounds.
The high-entropy-oxide OER behavior establishes a synergy similar to the proposed oxidized/reduced dual-site mechanism in PGM-catalyzed ethanol oxidation.
Concurrent oxidation-state changes in the high-entropy oxide support enhanced catalytic activity.
Inducing oxidation-state heterogeneity will increase ethanol-oxidation turnover frequency, improve selectivity toward complete oxidation or C–C-cleavage products, and enhance durability.
An overly oxidative pretreatment can homogenize the catalyst surface and thereby reduce catalytic performance.
The mechanism may fail at extreme potentials or when particle–support interactions dominate the catalytic response.
Particle morphology and support effects may modulate the influence of oxidation-state heterogeneity on catalytic kinetics.
